OUTSOURCE

1. Title + links

Kay Al Mannai · Yale School of Management · MGT 409 AI Foundations for Managers · November 23, 2026 (America/New_York).

Public repo: https://github.com/kalmanna3i/outsource

Application: run locally — streamlit run app.py (no production hosting in this submission).

OUTSOURCE is a Personal Strategy & Execution Office: it reads life goals, compares opportunity costs across competing obligations, assigns work to AI versus human, executes draftable work, and—when a barrier requires a person—prepares a private intervention brief, schedules a calendar slot, exports ICS, and resumes only after the user records an outcome.

This report describes a working prototype built by the author. Screenshots are from a real demo-mode run on the build machine (demo mode).

2. Motivation

Fictional persona (not a real pilot user)

Maya Chen is a fictional second-year MBA executive: she leads a small product team during the day, carries a 4.0 credit load, and is responsible for family logistics. On submission nights she faces four simultaneous pulls: a course final due at 11:59 PM Eastern, a close friend’s wedding with a fixed ceremony window, a stakeholder expecting a work status note, and an insurance claim stuck behind an identity-verification gate. Maya is competent; her bottleneck is not lack of intelligence but attention fragmentation and tools that optimize the wrong objective.

Today’s manual workflow (typical)

  1. Open the academic deliverable checklist in a notes app and mentally rank “MBA final” first without writing down tradeoffs against the wedding.
  2. Ask a general-purpose chat assistant for a priority list; receive fluent text with no persistent link to her stored goals or calendar conflicts.
  3. Draft a work email in the same chat thread; risk sending language she has not verified, or lose time merging versions across tabs.
  4. Open the insurer portal in a browser; hit knowledge-based authentication; stop without a prepared brief or a scheduled block on the calendar.
  5. Copy partial instructions into a calendar event—sometimes leaking claim identifiers into a description shared with an assistant’s calendar sync.
  6. After the call, forget to translate the outcome into follow-ups for the MBA and work threads.

Conservatively, this manual sequence involves fifteen or more context switches (apps, tabs, mental replans) before anything is “done.” Maya pays in three currencies: time (20–45 minutes of unstructured replanning on a deadline night), cognitive load (keeping four parallel state machines in working memory), and error risk (false completion—“ChatGPT said it checked the claim”—or privacy mistakes in calendar text). None of those costs appear on a profit-and-loss statement, but they show up as late submission risk, strained relationships, and compliance mistakes when claim identifiers leak into shared calendars.

OUTSOURCE does not replace Maya’s judgment on the MBA final or the wedding toast. It compresses the preparation surface area: one intake, one ranked plan, one explicit split of AI draft work versus human-only gates, and one resume step that records what the insurer actually said.

Why a manager should care

Knowledge workers do not need another drafting chatbot. They need a system that encodes which outcomes are non-negotiable, computes what each hour buys in goal terms, executes only what automation can honestly complete, and surfaces a single prepared human moment when the world requires ID, presence, or signature. OUTSOURCE is scoped to that pattern for Maya’s archetype; the builder (Kay) dogfoods the same submission-night scenario in the mandatory demo.

Design constraints implied by Maya’s evening

First, the academic final has a sharp external deadline—missing it is not negotiable, but parts of the work (outline, checklist, slide structure) can be drafted by AI while submission remains human. Second, the wedding is a fixed window: the system must treat it as an immovable busy block when searching for insurance-call slots. Third, the work obligation is urgent but not legally identity-gated—appropriate for draft generation plus human send approval. Fourth, the insurer path is explicitly a human-authentication wall in the demo fixture, standing in for portals that will not release PHI to an API. Any credible “chief of staff” software for Maya must represent those four obligation classes differently, not collapse them into a single prioritized to-do list.

From a managerial lens, the lesson generalizes beyond students: organizations routinely ask leaders to reason about opportunity cost without giving them software that records assumptions, tradeoffs, and who (human vs machine) should act. OUTSOURCE is a course-sized prototype of that recordkeeping discipline.

3. What is new here

Competition is real. Lindy, Motion, Reclaim, Duckbill, and OpenAI’s agent experiences all help individuals offload work. OUTSOURCE does not claim a green-field market; it occupies a narrower wedge: goal-weighted opportunity cost, explicit AI/HUMAN allocation, and a handoff contract that stops at identity walls instead of faking success. The table below lists only features this repository actually implements (verifiable in code/UI) versus publicly known positioning of named products—without asserting their internal architectures.

ProductWhat they are known forOUTSOURCE implements (verifiable in this repo)Still different here
LindyAI assistant / workflow automation for professionalsNo Lindy integration; local multi-agent orchestration in PythonLife Blueprint SQLite goals feed B01 opportunity-cost objects; not a hosted Lindy clone
MotionAI calendar and task auto-schedulingDeterministic find_slot with busy blocks, business hours, buffers—not ML schedulingSchedules human intervention after strategy agents, not generic task churn
ReclaimHabits, focus time, calendar defenseFixed wedding busy block seeded in workflow; slot search avoids overlapTradeoffs tied to academic/relationship/financial goals, not only focus habits
DuckbillHuman+AI concierge completing errandsNo human concierge staff; simulated insurer onlyTransparent local audit trail (Agent Activity, state transitions) for coursework
ChatGPT agentsGeneral tool-using agentsBounded specialist prompts + JSON handoffs + REVIEW_ALL permission gateInsurer path labeled SIMULATED_FIXTURE; WAITING_RESULT until user_result

The novelty for grading purposes is not “no competitors exist” but honest orchestration: separate public ICS text from private intervention fields, resume F06 only after user-supplied evidence, and default to demo fixtures that never masquerade as live model telemetry.

Lindy and similar “AI employee” products optimize for recurring business workflows (inbox, CRM, SDR tasks). OUTSOURCE deliberately does not integrate with corporate SaaS in this MVP; instead it stores a personal Life Blueprint locally so opportunity-cost comparisons reference your stated goals rather than a template industry vertical.

Motion and Reclaim are strong at calendar mechanics. OUTSOURCE’s scheduler is intentionally narrow—business hours, buffers, overlap detection—because the grading scenario is legibility and testability, not ML-optimized scheduling. The teaching point is scheduling in service of a human intervention that follows a strategy conversation, not scheduling for its own sake.

Duckbill sells outcome completion with humans behind the scenes. OUTSOURCE inverts the transparency model for education: every agent step is logged with mode=demo or live, and simulated insurer results are typed SIMULATED_FIXTURE in the evidence ledger.

ChatGPT agents (OpenAI’s agent modes and custom GPTs) can call tools broadly. Without hard constraints, they may summarize insurer status inaccurately. F03’s system prompt forbids claiming sends/calls; the workflow adds a Python gate that always routes insurer status through the fixture or a future real integration, never through unconstrained prose.

Handoff contract

Each specialist returns a single JSON object via LLMClient.complete. The orchestrator (WorkflowEngine) performs three mechanical steps: (1) append an AgentCallRecord to WorkflowState.agent_calls; (2) map JSON fields into Pydantic models (DecisionPlan, WorkPackage, HumanIntervention); (3) pass serialized prior objects as plain text inside the next agent’s user message. Demo mode injects fixtures tagged _demo_labeled; live mode uses OpenAI-compatible chat completions with response_format: json_object. The insurer step is not an LLM call—it is a Python function returning SIMULATED_FIXTURE evidence.

Downstream coupling example: B01’s recommended_sequence list is not merely displayed; F02’s prompt includes that list verbatim, and the UI’s My Decisions page renders the structured OpportunityCostItem rows rather than re-parsing free text. If a live model returned malformed JSON, the workflow would fail fast with an agent error recorded in Agent Activity—there is no silent fallback to fake success.

Permission insertion point: between F02 and F03, normalize_permission and may_auto_execute decide whether F03 runs at all. That is a different handoff from “model didn't feel like executing”; it is an explicit organizational control matching the MANAGED_AUTONOMY / REVIEW_ALL modes in the spec.

Model choice: why gpt-6-luna on the course key

Yale MGT 409 project requirements restrict the course Portkey key to gpt-6-luna only. OUTSOURCE defaults OPENAI_MODEL to that slug when PORTKEY_API_KEY is set without a personal OpenAI key. Eight short JSON completions per Priority 0 run favor a capable instruction-following model while remaining inside course budget rules. Personal OPENAI_API_KEY runs may set any model via OPENAI_MODEL. Demo submissions use zero model spend.

Structured outputs reduce parse failures: each specialist prompt enumerates required JSON keys, and the orchestrator assumes dict shapes when building Pydantic objects. That design trades a few extra output tokens for fewer orchestration bugs—important when teaching staff run the app once under time pressure.

5. Tokenomics

All dollar amounts below use measured data only when taken from a live API usage object. Demo runs are explicitly not measured.

Definitions

  • R = number of Priority 0 workflows per user per month (example: 20).
  • T_in, T_out, T_cached = tokens per workflow from provider usage (live only).
  • P_in, P_out = price per million tokens for the active model (from provider list price when known).
  • C_run = (T_in/10⁶)·P_in + (T_out/10⁶)·P_out (estimated if prices known).
ScaleFormulaDemo (this build)Live (requires measurement)
One runC_run from usageNot measured — 0 tokens, $0Fill from Agent Activity after one live run
Per user / monthR × C_run$0 at R=2020 × C_run
100 users / month100 × R × C_run$0linear scale; shared caching not modeled
10,000 users / month10,000 × R × C_run$0requires batching, prompt compression, caps
LIVE RUN PLACEHOLDER (not filled on build VM — no API key):
Input tokens: ______ · Cached input: ______ · Output tokens: ______ · Model: gpt-6-luna · C_run USD: ______ · Screenshot: Agent Activity page after live run.

Cost controls and tradeoffs

  • MAX_AGENT_CALLS (default 25) — hard stop before another completion; prevents runaway loops; may truncate unfinished workflows if set too low (tested at 3).
  • MAX_WORKFLOW_COST_USD (default 2.00) — accumulates estimated live spend only when usage+price table known; otherwise UNKNOWN.
  • APP_MODE=demo — zero spend for grading and screenshots; tradeoff: tokenomics section cannot show measured tokens without a live pass.
  • REVIEW_ALL permission — blocks F03 until checkbox approval; saves tokens but requires extra UI click (operational in tests).
  • Deterministic engines — insurer check, scheduler, ICS export, finance projection, safety regex scan run without LLM spend; tradeoff: insurer is simulation only.

If Maya ran live eight times per evening during exam season (unrealistic), monthly cost would be R × C_run with R ≈ 240; that stress case is why caps exist. Teaching staff grading in demo mode should expect not measured in the token column—this is correct behavior, not missing implementation.

Worked example (illustrative only — not measured): suppose a live Priority 0 run returned 12,000 input and 2,500 output tokens on gpt-6-luna, and staff recorded provider list prices P_in and P_out in dollars per million tokens. Then C_run = (12000/10⁶)P_in + (2500/10⁶)P_out. With R = 20 workflows/month, one user costs 20·C_run; 100 users cost 2,000·C_run; 10,000 users cost 200,000·C_run before engineering discounts. OUTSOURCE does not substitute guessed prices—leave the placeholder blank until Kay captures one live Agent Activity screenshot.

Operational notes on each defense

Injection quarantine is heuristic, not cryptographic: it pattern-matches instruction-override phrases and wraps the payload so downstream prompts treat content as data. Staff can verify by pasting attack strings into Daily Briefing or the Settings scanner.

REVIEW_ALL is enforced in code before F03, not merely described in documentation: a run without the Daily Briefing approval checkbox stops at PLANNED with a visible digital deliverable explaining the block (see permissions tests).

Spend caps increment only when live usage objects return token counts with a known price row; demo mode never increments cost, preventing accidental fabrication of “cheap” metrics.

7. Impact

No real pilot users were interviewed for this submission. Impact evidence is limited to builder-side measurements and structured comparisons.

Manual baseline vs OUTSOURCE (same four-obligation scenario)

DimensionManual baseline (fictional Maya workflow)OUTSOURCE demo run (wf_31b8c1ad3…)
Distinct planning artifacts~15 ad-hoc steps / context switches7 specialist calls + 1 fixture + 1 resume call = 8 logged agent steps
Structured work packagesNone persisted6 WorkPackage rows with assignee + status
Insurance completion without humanOften falsely assumedBlocked at WAITING_RESULT until user_result
Calendar artifactAd hoc event textICS file + private brief separation
Follow-upsMemory-dependent3 explicit strings from F06 after resume

Scheduler evidence from the same run

The workflow seeds a fixed wedding busy block (16:00–20:00 local naive time). The intervention slot was placed 09:45–10:15, respecting business hours and avoiding overlap with the wedding block—the deterministic engine’s purpose. Unit tests additionally cover overlap detection and impossible deadlines (tests/test_scheduler.py).

For course grading, the meaningful comparison is structural: manual workflows scatter state across tabs; OUTSOURCE persists a single WorkflowState with enumerated transitions, six packages, and an intervention object that must receive user_result before COMPLETED. That persistence is what teaching staff can replay in demo mode without inventing a pilot narrative.

Hours-saved or revenue figures are not claimed. A one-user timed study would be required to quote minutes saved credibly.

What teaching staff should expect when grading

Clone the public repository, optionally place a course .env one directory above the project folder, run streamlit run app.py, and execute the Priority 0 path in demo mode without spending tokens. Agent Activity should list eight calls after resume, each marked demo with UNKNOWN cost. If staff insert a real Portkey key and set APP_MODE=live, the same UI path should issue eight completions against gpt-6-luna; token fields populate only when the provider returns usage metadata. Staff should not expect email send buttons, live insurer APIs, or Network/Career modules—their absence is documented here rather than hidden.

One-month roadmap (if continued)

  1. Week 1: push public GitHub repo; one live run; fill token placeholder with screenshot.
  2. Week 2: Google Calendar OAuth read-only for real busy blocks.
  3. Week 3: email draft→approve→send behind MANAGED_AUTONOMY only.
  4. Week 4: three fictional-to-real pilot sessions with timed before/after protocol (still no invented quotes in reports).
